<div class="lead-note">
**About the data.** This report uses IBM's *HR Analytics Employee Attrition* sample:
1,470 **fictional** employees created by IBM data scientists. No real company or person
is described. I use it to show the method end to end in R; the numbers illustrate, they
do not describe a real workforce. All code is folded under the **Code** buttons, and the
same script produces the data behind the interactive version on my site.
</div>

```{r compute, echo = FALSE, ref.label = c("setup", "load", "segments", "model-data", "split", "logit", "validation", "survival", "survival-naive", "cox", "tree", "whatif", "insights")}
```

## Key findings

```{r key-findings, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
for (i in insights) cat(sprintf('<div class="finding"><b>%s</b>%s</div>\n', i$title, i$text))
```

## 1. The question and the data

Every exit costs a company twice: the work that stops while the seat is empty, and the
hiring and ramp-up of the replacement. HR leadership rarely has budget to fix everything,
so the useful question is narrower: **who leaves, when, and where would retention effort
pay off?**

The file has one row per employee: demographics, role and level, pay, tenure, travel,
overtime, four satisfaction ratings, and whether the person left (`Attrition`).
`r num(n_emp)` employees, `r num(n_left)` leavers: an attrition rate of
**`r pct(overall_rate, 1)`**. Three columns (`EmployeeCount`, `Over18`,
`StandardHours`) hold one value for everyone and are dropped. There are no missing values.

```{r show-load, ref.label = c("setup", "load"), eval = FALSE}
```

I look at the question through five lenses, each answering a different part of it:

| Lens | Question it answers | R tools |
|---|---|---|
| Segment rates + chi-square | Which groups leave more? | `dplyr`, `chisq.test` |
| Logistic regression | Which factors matter once the others are held constant? | `glm`, `broom` |
| Hold-out validation | Can we rank people by risk, and how well? | rank-based AUC, calibration |
| Survival analysis | *When* in their tenure do people leave? | `survival::survfit`, `coxph` |
| Decision tree | Which combinations of traits define high-risk pockets? | `rpart` |

A what-if on top of the regression then asks how many exits overtime might account for.

## 2. Who leaves? Attrition by segment

Each variable is cut into groups and tested with a chi-square test. Cramér's V puts
the strength of association on a 0-1 scale that is comparable across variables with
different numbers of groups.

```{r show-segments, ref.label = "segments", eval = FALSE}
```

```{r fig-segments, fig.height = 10}
seg_plot <- bind_rows(lapply(segments[1:8], function(s) {
  lv <- s$levels
  if (s$kind == "nominal") lv <- lv[order(lv$rate), ] else lv <- lv[rev(seq_len(nrow(lv))), ]
  data.frame(panel = sprintf("%s  (V = %.2f)", s$label, s$cramers_v),
             key = paste(s$key, lv$level, sep = "___"), lv)
}))
seg_plot$key   <- factor(seg_plot$key, levels = unique(seg_plot$key))
seg_plot$panel <- factor(seg_plot$panel, levels = unique(seg_plot$panel))
seg_plot$above <- ifelse(seg_plot$rate > overall_rate, "Above company average", "At or below average")

ggplot(seg_plot, aes(x = rate, y = key, fill = above)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.68) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), width = 0, orientation = "y", colour = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall_rate, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub(".*___", "", x)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = pct_axis, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Above company average" = blue, "At or below average" = "#c9c8c2")) +
  labs(title = "Attrition rate by group, the eight strongest variables",
       subtitle = sprintf("Bars: share who left, with 95%% Wilson intervals. Dashed line: company average (%s).",
                          pct(overall_rate, 1)),
       x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r tab-tests}
seg_tests %>%
  transmute(Variable = variable, `Chi-square` = round(chi2, 1), df,
            `p-value` = ifelse(p_value < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_value)),
            `Cramér's V` = round(cramers_v, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

All `r nrow(seg_tests)` variables differ significantly at the 5% level, which is
expected with 1,470 people. Effect size is the better guide, and the ranking is clear:
**overtime**, **job role**, **tenure**, **job level**, **age** and **pay** lead. Many of
these overlap: junior people are younger, newer and paid less. The regression
below separates them.

## 3. What predicts leaving, all else equal?

A logistic regression estimates each factor's effect while holding the others constant.
I chose an interpretable set of `r length(predictors)` predictors and left out
near-duplicates: monthly income tracks job level (r = 0.95), and years in role or with
the current manager track years at company (r ≈ 0.77). Gender is excluded on purpose.
Age and marital status stay in only as controls, so the effects of the levers HR can
act on are not confounded by them.

```{r show-logit, ref.label = c("model-data", "logit"), eval = FALSE}
```

```{r fig-or, fig.height = 5.8}
or_plot <- or_tab %>%
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)),
         sig = ifelse(significant, "Significant (p < 0.05)", "Not significant"))
ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = odds_ratio, y = label, colour = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), width = 0, orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Significant (p < 0.05)" = blue, "Not significant" = muted)) +
  labs(title = "Odds ratios from the logistic regression (all employees)",
       subtitle = "Right of 1 = higher odds of leaving. Lines: 95% profile-likelihood intervals. Log scale.",
       x = "Odds ratio", y = NULL)
```

```{r tab-or}
or_tab %>%
  transmute(Factor = label, `Odds ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", odds_ratio),
            `95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", ci_low, ci_high),
            `p-value` = ifelse(p_value < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_value))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

How to read it: **working overtime multiplies the odds of leaving by
`r sprintf("%.1f", or_tab$odds_ratio[or_tab$term == "Overtime"])`**, for two people who are
otherwise alike. Job level 1, low job involvement, poor work-life balance, working in Sales,
low environment satisfaction, having no stock options, frequent travel and low job
satisfaction all at least double the odds. Distance from home, the number of prior employers
and years since the last promotion add smaller amounts per unit; older age and longer tenure
lower the odds. Being single is no longer significant once stock options are in the model.
That is expected here: single employees in this sample *all* have stock-option level 0, so
the two effects share the same people and should be read together. Odds ratios also
overstate *risk* ratios when the outcome is common, so "5.9 times the odds" is not "5.9
times as likely".

## 4. How well can risk be ranked?

The same model was fitted on a 70% training split (stratified on the outcome,
`set.seed(2026)`) and scored on the `r num(nrow(test))` people it had never seen.

```{r show-validation, ref.label = c("split", "validation"), eval = FALSE}
```

* **AUC `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_test)`** on the hold-out (training `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_train)`;
  the small gap means little overfitting). Overtime alone reaches `r sprintf("%.2f", auc_ot_only)`.
  AUC is computed with the rank (Mann-Whitney) formula: the chance that a random leaver is
  scored above a random stayer.
* **Brier score `r sprintf("%.3f", brier)`** (mean squared error of the probabilities).

```{r fig-calib, fig.width = 4.6, fig.height = 4.2, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "49%"}
ggplot(calib, aes(mean_predicted, actual_rate)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = muted, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = blue, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = blue, size = 2.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = pct_axis, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct_axis, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Calibration by risk decile", subtitle = "Hold-out set; dashed = perfect calibration",
       x = "Predicted attrition", y = "Actual attrition")

ggplot(bind_rows(data.frame(share_flagged = 0, share_of_leavers = 0), gains),
       aes(share_flagged, share_of_leavers)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = muted, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = blue, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = filter(gains, abs(share_flagged - TOP_SHARE) < 1e-9), colour = orange, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = pct_axis) + scale_y_continuous(labels = pct_axis) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Leavers caught vs share flagged", subtitle = "Dashed = random flagging; dot = top 20%",
       x = "Share of employees flagged (riskiest first)", y = "Share of leavers caught")
```

The model ranks well but is not perfectly calibrated: the riskiest decile is
under-predicted and deciles 6-8 are over-predicted, about what one expects from
`r sum(test$left)` hold-out leavers. If HR flagged the **riskiest 20%** of the hold-out
group (predicted probability ≥ `r sprintf("%.2f", cm$threshold)`):

```{r tab-cm}
data.frame(` ` = c("Flagged (top 20%)", "Not flagged"),
           `Actually left` = c(cm$tp, cm$fn), `Stayed` = c(cm$fp, cm$tn), check.names = FALSE) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```

That list would contain **`r pct(cm$recall)` of the people who left**, and
**`r pct(cm$precision)` of the people on it would actually leave**, `r sprintf("%.1f", cm$lift)` times
the `r pct(cm$base_rate)` base rate. Useful for prioritising conversations; far too
uncertain to justify any decision about an individual.

## 5. When do people leave?

**A trap first.** The textbook Kaplan-Meier curve (time = years at company, stayers censored)
assumes we saw everyone's whole tenure. This file is a snapshot: it lists people who were
employed during one period and flags who left during it. People who left in earlier years
are not in it. The textbook curve still places every long-tenured stayer in the
first-year risk set, though nobody could have seen them leave in their first year a decade
ago. The result is a curve that hides early exits: it puts first-year retention at
**`r pct(ret_at(km_naive$overall, 1), 1)`**, while
**`r pct(exit_by_tenure$overall$rate[1])`** of the first-year employees in the file left.

**The fix is delayed entry** (left truncation). I assume `Attrition` covers one year (the
usual reading of this dataset), so someone with *k* completed years was at risk only
between tenure *k* and *k* + 1: `Surv(start = k, stop = k + 1, event)`. The curve then reads
as a synthetic cohort: *if this year's exit rates at each tenure held, what share of new
hires would still be here after t years?* The raw exit rate in each tenure year comes first,
because it needs no model at all.

```{r show-survival, ref.label = c("survival", "survival-naive"), eval = FALSE}
```

```{r fig-hazard, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(exit_by_tenure$overall, aes(x = factor(label, levels = label), y = rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = blue, width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall_rate, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = pct(rate)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.3, colour = ink2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct_axis, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Exit rate by tenure year", subtitle = "Share of employees in each year of tenure who left. Dashed: company average.",
       x = "Year of tenure (1 = first year)", y = NULL)
```

```{r km-helpers}
HORIZON <- 10
km_frame <- function(groups) bind_rows(lapply(groups, function(g) data.frame(group = g$group, g$curve))) %>%
  filter(time <= HORIZON)
km_plot <- function(df, colours, title, subtitle) {
  rects <- df %>% group_by(group) %>% arrange(time, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(xmax = lead(time, default = HORIZON)) %>% filter(time < HORIZON) %>% ungroup()
  ggplot(df, aes(time, surv, colour = group)) +
    geom_rect(data = rects, aes(xmin = time, xmax = xmax, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = group),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.12) +
    geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = colours) + scale_fill_manual(values = colours, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:HORIZON) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = pct_axis, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = "Years since joining", y = "Still employed")
}
```

```{r fig-km-ot}
km_plot(km_frame(km$by_overtime$groups), c(No = blue, Yes = orange),
        "Retention curve by overtime (Kaplan-Meier, delayed entry)",
        sprintf("Shaded: 95%% CI. Log-rank (score test) p %s.", fmt_p(km$by_overtime$logrank$p_value))) +
  labs(colour = "Overtime") + theme(legend.title = element_text(colour = ink2))
```

```{r fig-km-jl}
jl_cols <- setNames(c(blue, orange, aqua), levels(surv_df$JobLevel))
km_plot(km_frame(km$by_job_level$groups), jl_cols,
        "Retention curve by job level (Kaplan-Meier, delayed entry)",
        sprintf("Levels 3-5 pooled. Log-rank (score test) p %s.", fmt_p(km$by_job_level$logrank$p_value)))
```

```{r tab-retention}
ret_rows <- function(g) data.frame(Group = g$group, People = g$n, Leavers = g$events,
  t(setNames(ifelse(g$retention$reliable, pct(g$retention$surv), paste0(pct(g$retention$surv), "*")),
             paste("After", g$retention$year, ifelse(g$retention$year == 1, "year", "years")))),
  check.names = FALSE)
bind_rows(ret_rows(km$overall), lapply(km$by_overtime$groups, ret_rows), lapply(km$by_job_level$groups, ret_rows)) %>%
  mutate(Group = c("All employees", paste("Overtime:", c("No", "Yes")), levels(surv_df$JobLevel))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

`*` fewer than `r KM_MIN_RISK` people stood behind at least one step of that estimate
(only `r sum(surv_df$JobLevel == levels(surv_df$JobLevel)[3] & surv_df$YearsAtCompany == 0)`
people at levels 3-5 were in their first year), so it is not reliable.

The picture is consistent: **exits concentrate in the first two years**
(`r pct(t01$rate)` of employees in their first two years left, against
`r pct(t59$rate)` at 5-9 years), and **overtime workers leave sooner at every stage**.
Median time to exit for a synthetic new-hire cohort is
`r km$by_overtime$groups[[2]]$median_years` year for overtime workers and
`r km$by_overtime$groups[[1]]$median_years` years for everyone else. Compounding is what
makes these numbers look harsh: a 30% annual exit rate leaves fewer than 3% of a cohort after
ten years. They describe today's exit rates projected forward, not a real cohort.

```{r fig-naive, fig.height = 3.9}
cmp <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(version = "Textbook (no delayed entry)", km_naive$overall$curve),
  data.frame(version = "Delayed entry (used here)", km$overall$curve)) %>%
  filter(time <= HORIZON)
ggplot(cmp, aes(time, surv, colour = version)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Textbook (no delayed entry)" = muted, "Delayed entry (used here)" = blue)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:HORIZON) + scale_y_continuous(labels = pct_axis, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Same data, two retention curves", subtitle = "All employees. The textbook curve ignores that early leavers from past years are missing.",
       x = "Years since joining", y = "Still employed")
```

**Cox model.** A Cox proportional-hazards model with the same delayed entry asks which traits
make people leave *sooner at the same tenure*. The textbook version is shown for contrast:
without delayed entry, traits tied to short tenure (job level 1) look about twice as strong
as they are.

```{r show-cox, ref.label = "cox", eval = FALSE}
```

```{r fig-cox, fig.height = 4.2}
cox_plot <- cox_tab %>% left_join(cox_naive_tab, by = "term") %>%
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)))
ggplot(cox_plot, aes(y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), width = 0, orientation = "y", colour = blue, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(x = hazard_ratio, shape = "Delayed entry (used here)"), colour = blue, size = 2.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = hazard_ratio_naive, shape = "Textbook (biased)"), colour = ink2, size = 2.4) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Delayed entry (used here)" = 16, "Textbook (biased)" = 1)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8)) +
  labs(title = "Hazard ratios from the Cox model",
       subtitle = sprintf("Right of 1 = leaves sooner. Concordance %.2f; proportional-hazards test p = %.2f.",
                          cox_fit$concordance["concordance"], cox_zph$table["GLOBAL", "p"]),
       x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL)
```

The proportional-hazards assumption holds (global test p =
`r sprintf("%.2f", cox_zph$table["GLOBAL", "p"])`). Overtime has the largest effect
(**HR `r sprintf("%.1f", cox_tab$hazard_ratio[cox_tab$term == "Overtime"])`**), followed by
job level 1, low environment satisfaction and having no stock options.

## 6. Which segments are most at risk?

A decision tree finds combinations of traits with very different attrition rates. I grew a
regression tree on the 0/1 outcome (`rpart`, `method = "anova"`), so each leaf's mean *is*
its attrition rate, with at least 30 people per leaf, depth ≤ 4 and cp = 0.01 (ten-fold
cross-validated error falls at every retained split). A classification tree is the
usual choice, but on a 16% outcome it refuses to split the large low-risk branch, because
no split there changes the majority vote.

```{r show-tree, ref.label = "tree", eval = FALSE}
```

```{r tab-tree}
tree_leaves %>%
  transmute(Segment = rule, People = n, Leavers = leavers, `Attrition rate` = pct(rate),
            `vs average` = sprintf("%.1f×", lift), `Share of all leavers` = pct(share_of_leavers)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

Two pockets stand out: **overtime workers on the lowest pay** (`r pct(tree_leaves$rate[1])`
leave) and **overtime workers in lab, sales-executive and sales-rep roles with no stock
options** (`r pct(tree_leaves$rate[2])`). Together they are
`r pct(sum(tree_leaves$n[1:2]) / n_emp)` of employees but
`r pct(sum(tree_leaves$leavers[1:2]) / n_left)` of leavers. Without overtime, early-career
people (≤ 2 years of total experience) are the one high-risk group.

## 7. What if overtime were reduced?

Using the full-data logistic model, I take each of the `r num(n_ot)` overtime workers and
compare their predicted probability of leaving with the same person's prediction with
`Overtime` set to "No". Summing those differences gives the expected number of exits
associated with overtime. "Random" moves a share of overtime workers off overtime at random;
"targeted" starts with the people whose predicted risk falls the most.

```{r show-whatif, ref.label = "whatif", eval = FALSE}
```

```{r fig-whatif, fig.height = 4}
wi <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(scenario = "Random", share = scenarios$share, leavers = scenarios$expected_leavers_random),
  data.frame(scenario = "Targeted (largest drop first)", share = scenarios$share, leavers = scenarios$expected_leavers_targeted))
ggplot(wi, aes(share, leavers, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Random" = blue, "Targeted (largest drop first)" = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = pct_axis, breaks = OT_SHARES) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Expected leavers if overtime were removed for a share of overtime workers",
       subtitle = sprintf("Model-based, associational. Today: %s observed leavers.", num(n_left)),
       x = "Share of overtime workers moved off overtime", y = "Expected leavers")
```

```{r tab-whatif}
scenarios %>%
  transmute(`Share moved off overtime` = pct(share), `Workers` = workers_moved,
            `Expected leavers (random)` = sprintf("%.0f", expected_leavers_random),
            `Expected leavers (targeted)` = sprintf("%.0f", expected_leavers_targeted),
            `Attrition rate (targeted)` = pct(attrition_rate_targeted, 1)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "rrrrr")
```

Removing overtime altogether is associated with about **`r num(all_ot$reduction_random)` fewer
leavers** (`r num(base_expected)` → `r num(all_ot$expected_leavers_random)`). Targeting gets
most of that from half the workers: **`r num(half_ot$reduction_targeted)` fewer** when the
`r num(half_ot$workers_moved)` people whose predicted risk falls most come off overtime first.
The raw rate gap gives `r num(naive_reduction)`; the adjusted model lands close to it, so
the overtime effect is not explained away by who works overtime.

**On cost, I make no claim.** Replacement-cost estimates vary widely by role and company. The
leavers in this file earn on average `r num(cost_inputs$avg_monthly_income_leavers)` a month
(median `r num(cost_inputs$median_monthly_income_leavers)`, in the dataset's own units), and the
exits avoided in the full scenario belong to people earning about
`r num(cost_inputs$avg_monthly_income_avoided)` a month. If replacing someone costs *m* times
their annual pay, the full scenario is worth about
`r num(all_ot$reduction_random)` × 12 × `r num(cost_inputs$avg_monthly_income_avoided)` × *m*.
The interactive version on the site lets the reader set *m*, and set it against the cost of
the extra hiring that cutting overtime would need.

## 8. Recommendations: hypotheses for HR to test

None of these is proven by this analysis. Each is a hypothesis the data makes worth testing,
with a way to test it.

```{r recs, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
for (k in seq_along(recommendations)) {
  r <- recommendations[[k]]
  cat(sprintf("**%d. %s**\n\n", k, r$title))
  cat(sprintf("* *Hypothesis:* %s\n* *Action:* %s\n* *Measure:* %s\n* *Evidence here:* %s\n\n",
              r$hypothesis, r$action, r$measure, r$evidence))
}
```

## Reproduce

The analysis lives in one script; this report reads its chunks, so the numbers here and
on the site come from the same code.

```
Rscript analysis/people_attrition.R <ibm_attrition.csv> data
Rscript -e "rmarkdown::render('analysis/people_attrition.Rmd', params = list(csv = '<ibm_attrition.csv>'), output_dir = 'reports')"
```

The key findings and recommendations above are assembled from the computed numbers, not
typed in by hand:

```{r show-insights, ref.label = "insights", eval = FALSE}
```

The export step (it writes `data/attrition.js` and is not run while knitting):

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
```

pkgs <- c("dplyr", "survival", "broom", "rpart", "jsonlite", "ggplot2", "rmarkdown", "knitr")
cat(R.version.string, "\n")
cat(paste(pkgs, vapply(pkgs, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)), ""), collapse = " | "), "\n")
